1:
The book's new reign opens with a single word of policy — Jehoshaphat "strengthened himself against Israel" — and the witnesses read the young king's first act as at once shrewd statecraft and quiet faith. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott anchors the accession in the older record, noting that the opening clause repeats the last words of 1 Kings 15:24, and that the name itself means "Iah judgeth." The Israel against whom he strengthened himself is the northern kingdom; and these defensive measures, Ellicott is careful to add, belong to the early part of the reign, before Jehoshaphat ever linked himself by marriage to the northern dynasty, an alliance not formed until 2 Chronicles 18.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the rivalry behind the verse. The two kingdoms had contended from the beginning, now one prevailing and now the other; Asa and Baasha had been evenly matched, but after Baasha's death Israel was greatly weakened by civil contentions, and it was into that opening that Jehoshaphat stepped and gained the ascendancy, as the troubled Israelite succession of 1 Kings 16 records.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the political notice into a portrait of the man, and it is worth marking how carefully he qualifies the word "against." Jehoshaphat strengthened himself not to act offensively against Israel or to invade them, but only to maintain his own — fortifying his frontier cities and setting stronger garrisons in the towns of Ephraim he held. Ahab had by now been three years on the throne of Israel, an active, warlike prince whose vigour met the decay of Asa's last years, so that the northern kingdom had begun to grow formidable; the first thing the new king had to do was to make his part good on that side. And he did it, Henry observes, so effectually and without bloodshed that Ahab soon courted his alliance — proving in the end more dangerous as a friend than he could have been as an enemy. Above all Henry fastens on the manner of the strengthening: Jehoshaphat did not do as his father had done and buy security by a league with the king of Syria, but by fair and regular methods on which he might expect the blessing of God, and in which he trusted God.

The reformed John Gill passes the accession briefly — Jehoshaphat reigned in the stead of Asa his father — while the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch open with a survey of the whole reign that this verse begins, a king who laboured to strengthen his kingdom within and without, by garrisoned cities and a well-equipped army and, above all, by diffusing the knowledge of the law among his people. The witnesses do not divide; together they set the note the chapter will sound, that the surest strength of a throne is the favour of the God its king trusts.
2:
The strengthening of the previous verse now takes concrete military shape, and the witnesses attend to the network of garrisons the king threw across his land. The reformed John Gill reads it simply: he placed a considerable body of soldiers in all the fenced cities of Judah, to defend them should they be attacked. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fill in the Hebrew terms — chayil, forces, in the fortified cities, and netsibim, military posts, in the open land of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim which Asa his father had taken. These last, they note, point back to the conquests recorded earlier at 2 Chronicles 15:8, so that Jehoshaphat is consolidating ground his father had won.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, refines the vocabulary. "He placed forces" he compares with the like notice under Rehoboam at 2 Chronicles 11:12; the "fenced cities" are the walled towns already familiar from the fortifications of 2 Chronicles 11:5 and 2 Chronicles 14:6; and the "garrisons" he renders as military posts or prefects — the netsibim of 1 Chronicles 11:16 and 2 Chronicles 11:11 — the Syriac reading, more loosely, "appointed rulers." Whether the word denotes standing troops or the officers set over them, the picture is the same: a chain of manned strongpoints securing both the heart of Judah and its northern march.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke touches only the Ephraimite cities, and does so with an honest confession of the record's silence: this conquest from the kingdom of Israel is referred to at 2 Chronicles 15:8, but when it was made, he says, we do not know. The towns were Asa's gain from the north, and Jehoshaphat inherited and garrisoned them; the exact campaign that won them has dropped out of the history.

The witnesses do not divide, and Keil draws out the theology the bare notice implies. God blessed these undertakings — Jahve was with him — precisely because the king who built them walked in the ways of David and sought not the Baals, a link the next verse will make explicit. The garrisons are prudent, but their prosperity is not credited to prudence; the fortified frontier stands because the God of the frontier stood with the man who raised it. So the schools converge: Gill fixes the plain fact, Keil and Ellicott the terms and the strategy, Clarke the inherited conquest, and all of them let the fortification rest, in the end, upon the favour that made it prosper.
3:
Here the chapter names the secret of all the king's strength — "the LORD was with Jehoshaphat" — and the witnesses fasten on the reason the verse gives, that he "walked in the first ways of his father David." The reformed John Gill takes the divine presence in its fullest breadth: the Lord was with him guiding and directing, prospering and succeeding him in all things, granting him not only a powerful presence in his civil affairs but a gracious presence in spiritual things; and he notes the Targum's tender paraphrase, "the Word of the Lord was for his help" — a rendering the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke repeats, "the Word of the Lord was Jehoshaphat's Helper."

The weight of the verse, though, lies in that word "first," and here the witnesses reason closely. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds the distinction nowhere so strongly marked as here, between David's first ways and his last; for the last were not so good as the first. His earlier ways, before he fell so foully in the matter of Uriah — the one blot named long afterward as the bar in his escutcheon — were good ways; and though he happily recovered from that fall, perhaps he never, while he lived, fully retrieved the strength and comfort he lost by it. Jehoshaphat, then, followed David as far as David followed God, and no further — even as Paul would limit our imitation of himself in 1 Corinthians 11:1, "follow me, as I follow Christ." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it the same way: the first or earlier ways of David, as contrasted with his later conduct, a tacit allusion to the adultery with Bathsheba and the other sins of his last years told from 2 Samuel 11 onward. But Ellicott adds a textual note that Henry had also seen: a few manuscripts and the Septuagint omit the name David altogether, which would refer the "first ways" instead to Asa, Jehoshaphat's own father, in his earlier and better years before his late declension.

On the second half of the verse the witnesses are one. To "seek not unto Baalim," Ellicott explains, is to seek not the Baals — the local aspects of the sun-god — and the term here plainly reaches beyond Baal-worship proper to embrace the illegal worship of Jehovah under the form of a bullock, as Jeroboam had set it up and the north still practised it, "the doing of Israel" named in the verse that follows. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the Baalim are all false gods, and that the calf-cult by which Jahve was dragged down to their level falls under the same condemnation, as at Judges 2:11. So the debate that runs through the verse is only over whose "first ways" are meant — David's, on the received text, or Asa's, on the Greek — while over the thing praised there is no division at all: a king kept close to God by cleaving to the purer pattern of the past and refusing the idols of the present.
4:
Where the previous verse said what Jehoshaphat refused, this one says what he embraced — "but sought to the LORD God of his fathers, and walked in his commandments, and not after the doings of Israel" — and the witnesses read the two halves as a single, deliberate contrast. The reformed John Gill glosses the seeking plainly: he prayed to the God of his fathers, worshipped and served him. But the puritan eye catches the fuller shape of it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in "sought" the whole of true religion gathered up: Jehoshaphat worshipped the Lord God of his father, and him only; he prayed to him only and enquired of him only, both devotion and direction being included in the seeking. And more than worshipping the true God, he worshipped him according to God's own institution, and not after the doings of Israel — for though the king of Israel was his neighbour and his ally, he did not learn his way. Whatever dealings he had with him in civil matters, Henry insists, he would not have communion with him nor comply with him in his religion; in this he kept close to the rule.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the force of that closing phrase. Charles Ellicott identifies "the doings of Israel" precisely with the illegal worship of Jehovah under the form of a bullock, as Jeroboam had instituted it at 1 Kings 12:28 and the northern kingdom practised it — the very calf-cult the previous verse had folded under the name of the Baals. Keil and Delitzsch read the whole clause as the deliberate antithesis it is built to be: not merely that the king kept himself from false gods, but that he set his face against the entire pattern of the sister kingdom's worship, walking instead in the commandments the God of his fathers had actually given.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse rewards their attention because it draws the sharpest of lines. It would have been the easy and politic thing for a Judean king to drift toward the religion of the powerful northern court, especially once the two houses were bound by marriage; and Jehoshaphat's later entanglements would show how strong that pull could be. But here, at the outset, the historian records a king who sought the LORD and walked in his commandments precisely by not doing what Israel did. Gill fixes the seeking, Henry unfolds its exclusive devotion, Ellicott and Keil expose the corrupt "doings" it turned from. Between them they show that the positive and the negative are one act: to seek the God of the fathers is, in the same motion, to refuse the innovations of the calves, and it is on that undivided loyalty that the divine presence of the previous verse was seen to rest.
5:
The verse states the reward of the king's fidelity in three quick clauses — the kingdom established, presents brought, riches and honour in abundance — and the witnesses gather around each. The reformed John Gill makes the first a maxim of statecraft: piety is the best prop of government, and the throne is best supported and established by truth and righteousness and mercy; it was by the exercise of these that Jehoshaphat was settled in his kingdom and won a place in the hearts of his people. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the establishing with a cross-reference to the like notice at 2 Kings 14:5, and reads the word "therefore" as the hinge it is — the settled throne is the consequence of the sought God.

Over the "presents" a fine question arises, for the Hebrew minchah commonly means the tribute of subject peoples, as it will a few verses on when the Philistines pay it. Yet here, Ellicott and Keil agree, it cannot bear that sense. Ellicott takes it for the voluntary gifts of loyal subjects, such as were usual at the beginning of a reign, comparing the loyal offerings brought at Saul's accession in 1 Samuel 10:27; Keil and Delitzsch likewise insist the word here denotes not the regular imposts of subjects but freewill gifts brought as a token of reverence and love. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads them the same way — presents such as subjects in those times used to bring their kings, in token of their respect and subjection.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry alone ventures a reason for the giving, and links it to the reform the chapter is about to describe. All Judah brought him presents, he says, in acknowledgment of his kindness in sending preachers among them; for the more there is of true religion among a people, the more there will be of conscientious loyalty, and a government that answers the end of government will be supported. The effect of the favour both of God and of his people, Henry adds, was that he had riches and honour in abundance — and it is undoubtedly true, though few will believe it, that religion and piety are the best friends to outward prosperity. Keil sets the same clause beside the blessing of the great kings before him, for the phrase "riches and honour in abundance" recalls what was said of David at 1 Chronicles 29:28 and of Solomon at 2 Chronicles 1:12.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott ground the establishing of the throne in the king's piety; Ellicott, Keil, and Wesley read the presents as the freewill homage of a loyal people rather than exacted tribute; Henry alone tells us why they gave, tracing their loyalty to the religion the king had fostered. Together they let the verse make its quiet argument, that the God sought in the previous verses now visibly settles the kingdom, and that the wealth and honour crowning the reign are the overflow, not the origin, of a throne founded first upon devotion.
6:
The verse credits Jehoshaphat with a rare kind of boldness — "his heart was lifted up in the ways of the LORD" — and then with the act that boldness produced, the removal of the high places and groves. The grammatical-historical witnesses linger over the striking phrase. Both Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott observe that "his heart was lifted up" (gabhah leb) is almost everywhere a phrase of reproach, used of the haughty and the proud, as of Uzziah in his pride at 2 Chronicles 26:16. Here, uniquely, it is turned to praise: his courage rose high, he grew bold, in the ways of Jehovah and in the path of religious reform. The reformed John Gill reads the same note — his heart was engaged, bent, and set upon those ways, and he walked in them with pleasure and zeal, fearless and intrepid, regarding not the opposition his work of reformation was sure to meet. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley sums it in a phrase: his heart was lifted up above all discouragements and fears, valiant and resolute for God and his ways.

The courage bore fruit in demolition — "he took away the high places and groves out of Judah" — and here the witnesses must reckon with a difficulty, for the same book will later report that the high places were not taken away. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry offers the standard reconciliation: what he removed were those high places in which idols were worshipped, for those dedicated to the true God alone were not taken away, as the later notice at 2 Chronicles 20:33 allows; it was only idolatry that he abolished, and nothing had debauched the nation more than the idolatrous groves and images he swept away. John Wesley reaches the harmony from another side: Asa had done this work before him, yet either he had not done it thoroughly, or the people, many of them mad upon their idols, had secretly set up new ones in the latter and more infirm part of Asa's reign, so that there was fresh idolatry for Jehoshaphat to clear.

Ellicott hears in the connecting word "moreover" the same backward glance. It refers, he says, to the third verse — not only did Jehoshaphat not seek the Baals, but more than this, he removed their high places; or else, on a second reading he allows, "and he again removed," pointing back to Asa's earlier reforms at 2 Chronicles 14:3, which had since lapsed. The "groves," both grammatical-historical witnesses agree, are the Asherim, the sacred poles or trees of the Canaanite cult. So the witnesses converge without a jar. All read the "lifted-up heart" as holy courage rather than pride; all take the removal to touch only the idolatrous shrines, whether newly sprung up or left standing from a former reign; and together they portray a reformer whose inward boldness in God issued at once in the outward pulling-down of whatever rivalled him.
7:
In the third year of his reign Jehoshaphat launched the enterprise for which his name is chiefly remembered — a teaching mission sent through the cities of Judah — and the witnesses gather around its novelty and its careful composition. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke calls it plainly a remarkable account of an itinerant ministry, and marks that the king employed three classes of men in it: princes, Levites, and priests. The princes, he supposes, instructed the people in the nature of the civil law and the constitution of the kingdom; the Levites in all that pertained to the temple service and the ritual law; and the priests in the nature and design of the religion they professed. So the nation was thoroughly instructed in its duty to God, to the king, and to one another; the people became, he says, as one man, and against a people so united no enemy could prevail.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the make-up of the commission: five princes — that is, laymen of high position — sent with nine Levites and two priests into the cities of Judah, carrying the book of the law to teach it everywhere to the people. They are careful about the first name on the roll, insisting that Ben-hail is a proper name, formed like Ben-hesed and Ben-deker among Solomon's officers at 1 Kings 4:9, and not, as some render it, an adjective; the men are styled sarim, which suggests they were heads of families or fathers'-houses. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, agrees that the little word before the names marks them as the object of the verb — the king sent his princes, Ben-hail and Obadiah and the rest, to teach — and glosses Ben-hail as "son of valour," a compound name analogous to Ben-hur and the others of 1 Kings 4:8. None of the five, he notes, is otherwise known to us.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out how the princes taught. As judges instruct the people in the laws of the land when they deliver their charges from the bench, so these princes, in the king's name, admonished and required the people to observe and obey the laws of God, which were themselves the municipal laws of that land; the fuller explication and enforcement they left to the Levites and priests who went with them. The reformed John Gill adds only the grammatical possibility that the king "sent his princes" rather than "sent to" them, the particle serving here as the sign of the accusative.

The witnesses do not divide. Clarke lays out the three-fold teaching office, Keil and Ellicott secure the names and the composition, Wesley shows the princes wielding royal authority to summon the people to God's law, and Gill settles the grammar. Together they portray a king who understood that a people is governed best not by garrisons alone but by instruction — and who therefore sent the law itself, in the hands of his greatest men, into every city of his realm.
8:
To the princes the king joined the men whose office teaching properly was — "and with them he sent Levites... and with them Elishama and Jehoram, priests" — and the witnesses read the mixed commission as the heart of the whole design. The reformed John Gill notes simply that with the five princes went nine Levites, and with the Levites two priests. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch run through the roll of names and observe how the commission was framed: laymen of rank, Levites, and priests together, going about through all the cities of Judah with the book of the law of the LORD, teaching the people — a joint mission of the civil and the sacred orders.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, corrects the construction slightly — better "and with them were the Levites," the Septuagint and Syriac so reading — and remarks on the curious name Tob-adonijah, which occurs nowhere else and may be no more than an accidental doubling of the preceding Adonijah and Tobijah. He is most interested, though, in the phrase "the book of the law of the LORD." The writer plainly means the Pentateuch; and if this notice was drawn, as the chronicler tells us his account of the reign was, from the words of the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani at 2 Chronicles 20:34, it would stand as an important testimony to the existence — if not of the five books complete, then at least of an ancient collection of the Mosaic laws — at this early date, some eight hundred and fifty years before Christ. The commission, he adds, was a mixed one of civil and ecclesiastical persons, of the same character as the great mustered assemblies gathered under David at 1 Chronicles 24:6.

What binds the witnesses is the significance of that book carried from town to town. It was not the priests' own tradition nor the king's decree that the teachers brought, but the written law of God; and Keil is at pains that the volume is the Mosaic Pentateuch itself, not some later or partial code, since already in Jehoshaphat's time the law-book of Moses lay to hand as the authority to be taught. The teaching, both grammatical-historical witnesses agree, was no royal innovation dressed in religious language but the diffusion of an ancient and settled deposit — the priests and Levites doing at last, and under royal compulsion, the very work of instruction their office had always required of them.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill numbers the teachers, Keil names them and frames their circuit, Ellicott secures the text and draws from it his argument for the antiquity of the law. Between them they show the chronicler's deepest interest in the mission: that what went out into Judah was the book itself, the law of the LORD borne by the hands of priest and Levite and prince alike, so that a whole people might be governed by a word older than any of them.
9:
The verse describes the mission in motion — "they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people" — and the witnesses dwell on the book they carried and the effect it wrought. The reformed John Gill notes plainly that they taught the people their duty to God and to man. Recalling that teaching was the Levites' office by the ancient charge of Deuteronomy 33:10, the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on the detail that they had the book of the law with them, and finds in it a double purpose: it was for their own direction, that from it they might fetch all the instruction they gave and not teach for doctrines the commandments of men; and it was for the conviction of the people, that these might see the teachers had a divine warrant, and delivered to them only what they had received from the Lord. "Ministers," Henry draws the rule, "when they go to teach the people, should have their Bibles with them."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke unfolds the effect at length. This was their text-book — the book of God — and they taught it as such, and as such the people received it; its laws were God's laws, and the people felt their obligation and their consciences were bound. Thus they came to obey the laws of the land on the principle of religion, keeping the civil ordinances not merely for the sake of a good king but for the sake of a good and gracious God; and by these means the nation enjoyed peace and prosperity, and all seditions and popular commotions were prevented. Here Clarke cannot forbear an application closer to his own day: such an itinerant ministry, he urges, teaching the pure doctrines of the gospel together with the necessity of obedience to the laws, has been in his own age a principal means of preserving whole lands from the convulsions that have shaken the Continent — and he names the itinerant ministry established by the founder of the Methodists, whose followers, he says, are an honour to their country and a blessing to the government under which they live. It is a bold leap from Jehoshaphat's circuit-riders to the preachers of the eighteenth century, and it belongs to Clarke alone.

John Wesley, of the same school, is content to echo Henry — these itinerant judges and itinerant preachers together were instrumental to diffuse a blessed light throughout the cities of Judah. The witnesses do not divide over the substance. Gill fixes what was taught, Henry the divine warrant of the book and the rule for all who teach, Clarke the effect of a law-taught people and its parallel in his own century, Wesley the light that spread. Between them they show why the chronicler counted this mission the glory of the reign: a whole nation brought to obey God and king alike, not by force but by instruction, because the book of the law was carried into every city and opened before the people.
10:
The mission's reward was a peace no army had won — "the fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that were round about Judah, so that they made no war against Jehoshaphat" — and the witnesses agree that the dread was God's doing, not the king's. The reformed John Gill spreads the fear wide, over the ten tribes and the surrounding nations alike, Moabites and Edomites and Syrians, Egyptians, Arabs, and Philistines; and he traces it to their observing that religion was revived in Judah, for they had learned by long experience that the more religious this people were, the more prosperous and the more formidable. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the word — a dread of Jehovah — and reads the peace as the promised reward of piety, quoting the proverb that when a man's ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him, at Proverbs 16:7.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes this verse the very hinge of his reading of the reign. Jehoshaphat was not perhaps so great a soldier as David, which might have made him their terror, nor so great a scholar as Solomon, which might have made him their oracle; and yet the fear of the LORD so fell upon the neighbouring princes — God so influencing and governing their spirits — that they all revered him. None made war against him, for God's good providence so ordered it that, while the princes and priests were instructing and reforming the country, none of his neighbours gave him any molestation to take him off from that good work — even as the terror of God once fell upon the cities round about Jacob so that they did not pursue his sons at Genesis 35:5. And Henry presses the lesson home with all his force: it was not Jehoshaphat's formidable army that struck this terror into the nations, but the fear of God which fell upon them when he reformed his country and set up a preaching ministry in it. "The ordinances of God," he concludes, "are more the strength and safety of a kingdom than its military force — its men of God more than its men of war."

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the heathen reaction as a kind of rough theology: concluding from Jehoshaphat's singular piety that God would eminently appear for him, they dared not attack; for even the heathen could not but observe that the kings of Judah were prosperous or unhappy according as they served God or forsook him. The witnesses do not divide. Gill lists the awed nations and their reasoning, Ellicott names the peace a reward of piety, Wesley reads the nations' own inference, and Henry draws the governing maxim of the chapter. Together they turn a bare notice of peace into the argument the chronicler most wants pressed — that a kingdom's truest defence is the God whose fear its reformation had spread abroad.
11:
The dread of the previous verse now shows itself in gifts — the Philistines bringing silver, the Arabians their flocks — and the witnesses weigh both the payments and their character. The reformed John Gill supposes the Philistine tributaries to be those of Gerar and the neighbouring parts whom Asa had subdued and made to pay. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the whole as purchased peace: the Philistines and the Arabians alike bought the goodwill of the king of Judah by an annual tribute, the Philistines bringing silver and doubtless other merchandise, the Arabs — whose wealth lay in cattle — bringing flocks in great abundance, principally rams and he-goats.

Over the exact character of the payments the witnesses hover between homage and imposition. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the participle "brought" carries the force of a continual bringing, and that the word for the silver — massa, a load or burden — is a natural hyperbole, as if the Philistines paid "silver as much as they could carry," a usage he compares with the spoil of 2 Chronicles 20:25. Not all five Philistine states, he cautions, were subject to Jehoshaphat; and the Arabians here he takes for the nomad Bedouin whom Asa had conquered at 2 Chronicles 14:15, or else tribes that had come to acknowledge the king's overlordship, comparing the flocks Mesha of Moab rendered to Ahab at 2 Kings 3:4. Keil and Delitzsch simply register the tribute and pass to the greatness it betokened.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry threads the difference together. Many of the neighbouring nations, he says, brought presents to Jehoshaphat to secure his friendship; and perhaps these were a tribute originally imposed by Asa, who had made himself master of the cities of the Philistines and the tents of the Arabians at 2 Chronicles 14. He even fills in what the round figures omit: with the seven thousand seven hundred rams and the equal number of he-goats that the Arabians brought, there was in all likelihood a proportionable number of ewes and lambs, she-goats and kids — a whole levy of the flock, not merely its males.

So the witnesses circle a single scene from slightly different angles: was this the freewill homage of frightened neighbours, or the continued exaction of a tribute Asa's conquests had first imposed? Gill and Henry lean toward an inherited tribute; Clarke calls it purchased peace; Ellicott hears in the very words the picture of subjects staggering under loads of silver. But none doubts the point the chronicler is making — that the fear of the LORD which had fallen upon the nations translated, in hard silver and driven flocks, into the visible enrichment of a godly king, so that even the wealth of Judah's enemies flowed in to swell the prosperity that piety had secured.
12:
The verse gathers the whole growth of the reign into one swelling clause — "Jehoshaphat waxed great exceedingly" — and then names the works that measured it. The reformed John Gill takes the greatness broadly: he waxed great in wealth and riches, in power and authority, in his forces and his fortifications. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the Hebrew more exactly as a continuous advance — "he was going on and waxing great," becoming greater and greater — and notes that the phrase for "exceedingly," ad lemalah, is a rare one, occurring only here and at 2 Chronicles 16:12 and 2 Chronicles 26:8 in all the Old Testament.

The building that expressed this greatness draws the philologists' care. Like his predecessors Solomon, Rehoboam, and Asa, Ellicott observes, Jehoshaphat displayed his wealth and power in great public works — much as the records of the Assyrian and Babylonian sovereigns are largely taken up with the building of temples and palaces. The "castles" he built are the biraniyoth, a word derived from the term for a fortress or citadel and marked by its Aramaic form, recurring only at 2 Chronicles 27:4; Keil and Delitzsch describe them as castles or strongholds, and take the "cities of store" beside them for the magazine-towns familiar from Solomon's reign at 2 Chronicles 8:4. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same building program with a homely image: the king pulled down his barns and built larger, raising castles and cities of store for both arms and victuals; he was a man of business who aimed at the public good in all his undertakings, whether to preserve the peace or to prepare for war.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse repays their attention because it shows how the chronicler conceives of greatness. It is not conquest that measures Jehoshaphat's exceeding advance, but construction — fortresses to guard the realm and storehouses to provision it. Gill fixes the many dimensions of the greatness, Ellicott and Keil the exact sense of the terms and the company of builder-kings in which Jehoshaphat stands, Henry the practical wisdom of a ruler stockpiling against the day of need. Together they portray a king whose prosperity did not run to display or ease but to the sober strengthening of his kingdom, castle by castle and store by store — the outward fabric, raised in the years of peace that the fear of the LORD had bought, of a realm bracing itself in quiet for whatever should come.
13:
A single obscure word governs the first half of this verse, and over it the witnesses genuinely divide. The clause reads "he had much business in the cities of Judah," and the question is what the Hebrew melakah here means. The reformed John Gill takes it of activity — the king had much to do in his cities, partly in fortifying them and partly in reforming their inhabitants. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read it the same way: Adam Clarke understands that Jehoshaphat kept the people constantly employed, paying them wages for their work, so that by their labours the kingdom was both enriched and strengthened; and John Wesley glosses the "business" as the repairing and fortifying of the cities, the furnishing of them with provisions, and the purging out of every relic of idolatry and injustice.

The grammatical-historical witnesses will have none of it. Keil and Delitzsch insist, with Luther, that the word is rightly rendered "much store" — melakah denoting here, as in the law of the deposited goods at Exodus 22:7, property or produce gained by work. The rendering "much work," they argue, suits neither the context nor the parallel second half of the verse, for the labour of equipping the cities answers nothing to "the mighty men of valour in Jerusalem"; the only fit parallel is the goods and property stored in those cities, the provision of victuals and war-material laid up there. Charles Ellicott agrees precisely — not "business" but "much goods, or stores," the same word used of a neighbour's goods at Exodus 22:10 — so that the verse describes not the king's busy labours but his stocked magazines of provision and arms.

On the second half the witnesses close ranks. The "men of war, mighty men of valour," who "were in Jerusalem" are not, Ellicott explains, the whole army corps whose vast numbers the following verses will give, but simply their chiefs — the commanders who kept their station at the capital about the king. Keil takes the same view, using the clause as the doorway into the great muster that follows, the men fit for war reviewed according to their fathers'-houses.

So the verse leaves one honest disagreement standing. Was Jehoshaphat's "much melakah" the ceaseless business and public works of an industrious reign, as Gill, Clarke, and Wesley read it, or the heaped-up stores of a well-provisioned kingdom, as Keil and Ellicott insist against the older versions? The difference is real, turning on a word that can bear both senses; yet it does not touch the drift of the passage, which either way portrays a king whose cities were full — whether of labour or of goods — and whose captains stood ready at Jerusalem. And with that mention of the men of war the historian turns from the fabric of the kingdom to the force that manned it, and the roll of Jehoshaphat's armies begins.
14:
The chapter now unrolls a muster-roll of Jehoshaphat's forces, and the witnesses attend to its order and its head. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains the principle of the list: this is the army's census, taken according to the fathers'-houses or clans, as at 1 Chronicles 24:3; the warriors were marshalled by their stock, so that men of the same kindred fought side by side. He suspects that in the original document this heading was followed by a much fuller scheme of names and divisions than the text now preserves. "Of Judah" belonged the captains of thousands — three of them, named in the verses here — and Adnah the chief, whom Ellicott takes for the commander-in-chief of the whole host, both because he is named first and because his corps is the largest.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the same structure: the men fit for war passed in review by their fathers'-houses, the male strength of Judah falling into three divisions and that of Benjamin into two. Adnah held the first place among the generals, with three hundred thousand men of Judah; the phrase that he had others "at his hand" they take to mean with and under him, so that Jehohanan commanded two hundred and eighty thousand and Amasiah two hundred thousand beneath the chief. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke does the plain arithmetic, calling Adnah the generalissimo of all this host and reckoning the five battalions in order — three hundred thousand under Adnah, two hundred and eighty thousand under Jehohanan, two hundred thousand under Amasiah, two hundred thousand under Eliada, and a hundred and eighty thousand under Jehozabad — one million one hundred and sixty thousand in all. The reformed John Gill notes only that the reckoning runs first through Judah and then through Benjamin, by the house of their fathers.

The witnesses do not divide, and their agreement lets the roll do its work. What the chronicler gives is not a chaotic levy but an ordered army, drawn up tribe by tribe and clan by clan under named commanders, with the greatest of them, Adnah, at its head. Ellicott secures the principle of the muster and Adnah's primacy, Keil the three-and-two divisions and the chain of command, Clarke the tally of the battalions, Gill the tribal order. Between them they set before the reader the martial strength of a reign whose truer strength, the chapter has already insisted, lay not in these hundreds of thousands but in the fear of the LORD that had made war against Judah needless — a point the very hugeness of the coming totals will only underline.
15:
The second of Judah's captains is named — "next to him was Jehohanan the captain, and with him two hundred and fourscore thousand" — and a small but real question opens over that phrase "next to him." The reformed John Gill reads it as no mark of rank at all: Jehohanan was of the same office as Adnah, only with a lesser number of men under him, and the words may respect not any kind of subordination but merely nearness of place, as the Targum has it, "he that encamped next to him." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it otherwise — "at his hand," that is, beside him and subordinate to him, as the like phrase is used at 1 Chronicles 25:2 — and Keil and Delitzsch agree, having already taken the same idiom in the previous verse to mean "with and under him." So the witnesses divide, mildly, over whether the roll descends a chain of command or simply lists co-ordinate captains in the order of their encampment. The stakes are slight but not nothing: on Gill's reading the great commanders stand as equals, each over his own division; on the reading of the grammatical-historical pair they form a graded staff descending from Adnah the chief.

Keil and Delitzsch use this place to raise the harder problem the whole muster presents — the sheer size of the figures. Adding the divisions of Judah, they reckon seven hundred and eighty thousand warriors capable of bearing arms in that tribe alone; and these figures, they own, are clearly too large, bearing no proportion to the count of David's day, when Judah could muster but five hundred thousand or fewer, as the census of 1 Chronicles 21:5 set against the parallel at 2 Samuel 24:9 makes plain. Yet the sums of the single divisions, they add, are duly proportioned one to another — a fact that makes it the harder to dismiss the whole as a mere slip of the pen, and that leaves the difficulty standing for the fuller discussion the end of the chapter will draw out.

The witnesses do not, in the end, part company over anything vital. Gill and the grammatical-historical pair differ only on a shade of the idiom — whether "at his hand" ranks Jehohanan beneath Adnah or merely sets him beside him — and even Keil's frank admission that the totals are too large is offered not to discredit the record but to be reckoned with honestly. Between them they carry the roll forward: a second great division of two hundred and eighty thousand men under a named captain, whether subordinate or co-ordinate, and behind the tidy figures the honest scholar's question, already raised, of how so small a kingdom could field so vast a host — a question the closing verse will meet head-on.
16:
Of all the captains in the roll only one is given a word of character, and the witnesses pause where the chronicler pauses — on Amasiah the son of Zichri, "who willingly offered himself unto the LORD." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the most of it. Amasiah offered himself, he says, not only to the king, to serve him in this post, but to the LORD, to glorify him in it; he was the most eminent among the commanders for religion, and he accepted his place not for its honour or power or profit but for conscience' sake toward God, that he might serve his country. It was usual, Henry notes, for great generals to offer of their spoils to the LORD, as of the dedicated things at 1 Chronicles 26:26; but this good man offered himself first to the LORD, and then his dedicated things after.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott brings his usual philology and draws from it a larger point. The name Amasiah, he explains, means "Iah carrieth," and is to be distinguished from the similar Amaziah, "Iah is strong"; the phrase "willingly offered himself" is the language of freewill devotion heard in Deborah's song at Judges 5:9. Above all, Ellicott sees in this passing commendation an allusion to some noble act of self-devotion, doubtless more fully recorded in the source from which the chronicler drew his brief account. Such allusions, he argues, though their particulars are now lost to us and no longer intelligible, are important precisely as evidence — for they show that the narrative rests upon real records, dropping here a name and a praise whose full story the writer plainly knew. Keil and Delitzsch make the same observation more soberly: it is not communicated why it should be so honourably recorded of Amasiah that he offered himself willingly, the reason having fallen away with the fuller source.

The reformed John Gill notes only, with the Targum, that Amasiah encamped next to the captain before him, taking the connective in the same spatial sense he had given it in the previous verse. The witnesses do not divide, and the verse rewards their care because it lets a single soldier's piety shine out of a bare military list. Henry unfolds the devotion — a man who gave himself, and not merely his goods, to God; Ellicott and Keil mark the lost story behind the praise and turn even that loss into a proof of the record's authenticity; Gill fixes the man's place in the line. Between them they show why the chronicler, hurrying through his hundreds of thousands, stopped for one name: because here, in the midst of an army mustered for the defence of the realm, was a commander who understood that the truest offering a man can bring is not his spoils but himself.
17:
The muster crosses from Judah into Benjamin, and the witnesses turn to Eliada and the famous archers he led — "a mighty man of valour, and with him armed men with bow and shield two hundred thousand." The reformed John Gill marks Eliada simply as the chief commander of the Benjamite contingent. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the armament from the Hebrew: literally these were men "drawing bow and shield," which the Targum unfolds as "drawing the bow and grasping shields"; the Septuagint calls them archers and targeteers, the Vulgate men grasping bow and shield. The description, he notes, is of a piece with the ancient character of the tribe, whose warriors are elsewhere reckoned as mighty men of valour and archers at 1 Chronicles 8:40, and who could handle bow and sling with either hand at 1 Chronicles 12:2.

Keil and Delitzsch set Eliada's division within the structure of the Benjamite force, which fell, they say, into two detachments — these archers with shields, two hundred thousand strong, and a second body, differently armed, whom the next verse will name. The distinction is worth marking: Benjamin, the small tribe wedged between Judah and the northern kingdom, brought to the muster not one undifferentiated mass but a force ordered by its manner of arms, its renowned bowmen counted apart from the rest. Two hundred thousand strong, this single Benjamite battalion nearly matched the largest divisions of Judah — a striking weight of archery from so small a tribe.

The witnesses do not divide, and the little that they say opens onto the long memory of the tribe. Benjamin had been a byword for its archers and slingers since the days of the Judges, when its left-handed men could sling a stone at a hair's breadth and not miss; and here, generations later, the same martial inheritance stands mustered under Eliada in the service of a Davidic king. Gill names the commander, Ellicott secures the armament and its tribal pedigree, Keil sets the division in its place among the two bands of Benjamin. Between them they show the chronicler doing for Benjamin what he did for Judah — numbering not a rabble but an ordered army, each division under its captain and known by its weapons — and they let the reader feel, in the bows and shields of these two hundred thousand, the weight of a tribe's ancient prowess laid at the disposal of a reign that, for all its arms, would boast that its real defence was the fear of the LORD.
18:
The second Benjamite division completes the roll — "next to him was Jehozabad, and with him a hundred and fourscore thousand ready prepared for the war" — and over the meaning of that last phrase the witnesses quietly disagree. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the words "equipped for service" and takes the men to be the heavy-armed infantry, the hoplites of the host, comparing the like expression for the armed and ready at 1 Chronicles 12:23 and the mustering for war at Numbers 31:5. Keil and Delitzsch read the same Hebrew the other way: these were not the heavy-armed, as one commentator would have it, but simply men "equipped of the army" — provided, that is, with the usual weapons of sword and spear and shield, after the manner of the armed bands at 1 Chronicles 12:24. So a small technical question stands between them: were Jehozabad's hundred and eighty thousand the specially heavy-armed foot, distinguished from Eliada's bowmen by their weight of armour, or merely the ordinary armed levy, distinguished from the archers only in that they carried the common close-quarters weapons rather than the bow? The difference is one the ancient world felt keenly, for an army's order lay largely in the sorting of its arms — bowmen apart from spearmen, light apart from heavy — and the chronicler's care to distinguish the two Benjamite bands is itself a mark of a genuine muster-roll rather than a round invention.

The reformed John Gill, as before, takes the opening words in their plainest sense, noting only with the Targum that Jehozabad encamped next to the captain before him. Neither he nor the others makes the disagreement a quarrel; it turns wholly on the force of a single military term, and either way the picture is much the same — a second great body of Benjamite troops, differently armed from the first, drawn up under its own commander.

With this division the muster closes, and the witnesses let the completed roll speak. Benjamin, reckoned in its two detachments, brought three hundred and eighty thousand men to the field; Judah had furnished seven hundred and eighty thousand more; and the whole array stood ordered tribe by tribe and division by division, each under a named captain, the archers and the armed foot of Benjamin counted as carefully as the great battalions of Judah. Ellicott and Keil dispute only how heavily Jehozabad's men were armed; Gill fixes the man's place in the line. Between them they bring the long enumeration to its end and set the stage for the summary verse that follows, where the standing forces about the king will be distinguished from the garrisons of the fortified cities, and where the staggering sum of the whole — well above a million men — will at last provoke the question the honest reader has been waiting to ask: how so small a land could raise so vast a host.
19:
The roll ends with a distinction and a staggering sum — "these waited on the king, beside those whom the king put in the fenced cities throughout all Judah" — and the witnesses close the chapter by reckoning with both. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the sense of "waited on": these are they that ministered unto the king, the five generals just named, distinguished from the commandants whom he had set over the fortresses of the realm, such as those noted under Rehoboam at 2 Chronicles 11:11. Both alike are called the king's "ministers," a word not used of service in the field but implying attendance at court — the royal staff in Jerusalem. The reformed John Gill reads the waiting as done in course, the captains and their detachments serving by turns as David's men had, ready at the king's command whenever he had need; and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that these were the trained bands whose chief officers waited on the king to receive his orders and to raise their forces as occasion required, the men themselves dispersed through the country, each on his own land, but ready at call.

It is the sum of them — seven hundred and eighty thousand of Judah, three hundred and eighty thousand of Benjamin, some eleven hundred and sixty thousand in all — that raises the great difficulty, and here the witnesses reason in earnest. Ellicott states it squarely: these are the largest totals assigned to the two tribes anywhere in Scripture, far outrunning David's census of five hundred thousand men of Judah at 2 Samuel 24:9, and outrunning too the army of three hundred thousand and two hundred and eighty thousand that Asa had fielded at 2 Chronicles 14:8; such an increase, he owns, is unaccountable. Yet the figures are plainly no accident of the copyist, for they descend in the exact order of relative strength and are evidently bound up with Asa's earlier estimate. Ellicott's own resolution is to read them not as an army that ever mustered in the field but as an estimate of the total male population liable to be called out for the national defence — though even so, he confesses, the sum appears at least three times too great for so small a country.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley meet the same difficulty with the resources of faith and history. It was a vast number, they grant, for so small a compass of ground to furnish and maintain; but God had promised to make the seed of Abraham as the sand of the sea for number; there had now been a long peace; many had come over from the kingdom of Israel to swell the population, as the great defection to Asa at 2 Chronicles 15:9 records; and Jehoshaphat was under a special blessing of God that made his affairs to prosper greatly. Adam Clarke, for his part, will not leave the chapter without a statesman's application: it shows, he says, that true religion is the basis of the state, and that a religious nation is ever great, loved by its friends and dreaded by its enemies.

The witnesses do not, in the end, divide over the fact. Together they bring the long chapter to rest where it began, upon a kingdom made strong; and they leave the reader with the chronicler's settled conviction that the true secret of that strength was never the eleven hundred thousand swords, but the God whose fear had, for a season, made them needless.
